Police oversight reports and open data

Source: vignettes/oversight-reports.Rmd
oversight-reports.Rmd

Reading the text of police oversight reports into fields, and loading tables of the project’s open data service.

Each section is one help page: what the function is for, the example of its help page as it runs, and the plot of its result where the package draws one. ?name gives the arguments and the value in full.

Police oversight reports

Text of a police oversight report

ovrtxt(): Turns the page of a report published by a police oversight body (a civilian investigation unit, an ombudsman, an inspector) into the plain text its other tools read: markup removed, each paragraph, heading, list item and table row on a line of its own, so that section headings stand alone, and character entities decoded. Use it to read or search saved reports without a browser, or before the rules that code them.

ovrtxt("<h2>The Team</h2><p>Number of investigators assigned: 3</p>")
#> [1] "The Team\n\nNumber of investigators assigned: 3"
ovrtxt("<p>WO\n#1 Interviewed</p><p>WO&nbsp;#2 Interviewed</p>")
#> [1] "WO #1 Interviewed\n\nWO #2 Interviewed"
ovrtxt("a  b\r\nc", html = FALSE)
#> [1] "a b\nc"

Dates written out in reports, as ISO dates

ovrdte(): Finds the first date written in each text, in English or French, and gives it as YYYY-MM-DD, the form that sorts and that as.Date() reads. "January 5, 2023", "Jan. 5th 2023", "5 January 2023", "5th of January, 2023", "5 janvier 2023" and "2023-01-05" all give "2023-01-05".

ovrdte(c("January 5, 2023", "le 1er février 2021", "no date"))
#> [1] "2023-01-05" "2021-02-01" NA
ovrdte("On February 30, 2023 or rather March 2, 2023, the SIU ...")
#> [1] "2023-03-02"
as.Date(ovrdte("Date: April 28, 2023"))
#> [1] "2023-04-28"

Field schemas for coding police oversight reports

ovrsch(): The fields a preset reads from each report, and the rule, cues and section of each: a data frame that ovrpar() takes as schema. Copy it and change rows, or write one of the same columns, to code the reports of any oversight body; nothing in the rules is tied to one agency.

s <- ovrsch()
s[, c("name", "rule")]
#>                             name   rule
#> 1                    case_number  after
#> 2                 police_service   name
#> 3           date_of_incident_iso   date
#> 4          date_siu_notified_iso   date
#> 5  date_of_director_decision_iso   date
#> 6              siu_investigators    num
#> 7    siu_forensics_investigators    num
#> 8    number_of_witness_officials    tag
#> 9   number_of_civilian_witnesses    tag
#> 10   number_of_subject_officials    tag
#> 11                  age_affected before
#> 12           sex_gender_affected   word
#> 13           charges_recommended   flag
#> 14                directors_name   prev
#> 15              location_of_call  after
#> 16             specific_injuries   sent
#> 17          relevant_legislation  lines
# a field of one's own: the date a complaint came in
s2 <- rbind(s, data.frame(name = "date_received", rule = "date",
                          cue = "received the complaint", alt = "",
                          sect = "",
                          desc = "the date the complaint came in"))
tail(s2[, c("name", "rule", "cue")], 2)
#>                    name  rule                    cue
#> 17 relevant_legislation lines                Section
#> 18        date_received  date received the complaint

Code police oversight reports into fields

ovrpar(): Reads the fields of a schema from each report: the dates, the counts of officials and witnesses, the service, the outcome and whatever else the schema names, each by its rule (see ovrsch()). The rules are deterministic and offline, so the same report always gives the same row, and a folder of saved reports becomes a data set whose every value can be traced to the words that gave it.

r <- paste(
  "<h1>Director's Report - Case # 23-OFD-001</h1>",
  "<p>On January 6, 2023, the Barrie Police Service contacted the SIU.",
  "In the night, a 34-year-old man was injured.</p>",
  "<p>Number of SIU Investigators assigned: 3</p>",
  "<p>WO #1 Interviewed</p><p>WO #2 Interviewed</p>",
  "<p>Joseph Martino</p><p>Director</p>"
)
p <- ovrpar(r)
p[, c("case_number", "police_service", "date_siu_notified_iso",
      "siu_investigators", "number_of_witness_officials",
      "age_affected", "directors_name")]
#>   case_number        police_service date_siu_notified_iso siu_investigators
#> 1  23-OFD-001 Barrie Police Service            2023-01-06                 3
#>   number_of_witness_officials age_affected directors_name
#> 1                           2           34 Joseph Martino

The number of subject officials in an oversight report

ovrsoc(): Counts the subject officials of each report, the officers whose conduct the oversight body investigated, and says which rule gave the count and on what words, so that the number can be checked against the report. Use it where a report has no roster ovrpar() can read, or to check a count coded by hand.

ovrsoc(c("Subject Officials\nSO #1 Interviewed\nSO #2 Declined",
         "Two subject officials were designated.",
         "Witness Officials\nWO #1\nWO #2",
         "No officers are named here."))
#>   count rule                                      reason
#> 1     2    1 the roster under the heading: highest SO #2
#> 2     2    3           a plural: 'Two subject officials'
#> 3     0    5               witness officials only: WO #2
#> 4    NA    6                                  unresolved

Keyword indicators in oversight reports

ovrkwd(): Marks each report that mentions any word of each keyword group: the signals of mental health and of race that analyses of oversight reports tally, or any groups of one’s own. A mention is a signal to read the report, not a finding: a report may name a condition only to rule it out.

x <- c("The man had a history of schizophrenia; a crisis team came.",
       "An Indigenous woman was arrested.",
       "Nothing of either kind.")
k <- ovrkwd(x)
k
#>   mental_health  race        terms
#> 1          TRUE FALSE schizophren*
#> 2         FALSE  TRUE   Indigenous
#> 3         FALSE FALSE
colSums(k[c("mental_health", "race")])
#> mental_health          race 
#>             1             1
ovrkwd(x, list(force = c("taser", "conducted energy weapon", "baton")))
#>   force terms
#> 1 FALSE      
#> 2 FALSE      
#> 3 FALSE

Check a coded table of oversight reports

ovrchk(): Flags the cells of a table coded from oversight reports (by ovrpar(), by hand, or by any other means) that are not of the form their field calls for, so that a parsing slip or a typing error is found before the table is analysed. Nothing is changed.

d <- data.frame(case_number = c("23-OFD-001", "23-OFD-1", NA),
                date_of_incident_iso = c("2023-01-05", "2023-02-30", ""),
                number_of_subject_officials = c(1, 2.5, NA),
                charges_recommended = c(FALSE, NA, TRUE))
ovrchk(d, shape = c(case_number = "99-AAA-999|99-AA-999"))
#>   row issues
#> 1   1      0
#> 2   2      3
#> 3   3      0
#>                                                                                 what
#> 1                                                                                   
#> 2 date_of_incident_iso: date; number_of_subject_officials: count; case_number: shape
#> 3

Open data

Tables of the open data service

odtab(), odls(): odls() lists the tables of the project’s open data service and odtab() loads one by its key, as the service serves it at the time of the call. Everything about a table (its address, rows, columns and SHA-256) is read from the service’s manifest at run time, so a table that its publisher has replaced is loaded as it is now, with no new release of crimlab.
